narrative:
The model predicted a 66.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students, signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in your studies. Your first-year ranking had the next largest impact, also pulling the outcome toward failure; again you placed in the lowest decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. These two performance signals outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.60 it sits noticeably above the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the two weak class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 31, family income in the lower-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the overall picture.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in any future coursework, consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score, and then reapply. Many students strengthen their profiles in a second cycle and gain admission.
